label: Person
name: Acca of Hexham
summary:
Acca of Hexham (660–742) was a Northumbrian bishop who served as Bishop of Hexham from 709 to 732, a leading figure in the golden age of Northumbrian Christianity that produced Bede, Wilfrid, and Cuthbert. Born in Northumbria, he studied under Bosa of York before becoming the companion and close associate of Bishop Wilfrid of York — the most controversial and dynamic figure in early English Christianity.

Acca accompanied Wilfrid on his remarkable journeys to Rome and Frisia, and when Wilfrid died in 709, Acca succeeded him at Hexham. His episcopate established Hexham as an important centre of learning and liturgical excellence. He built up the cathedral's library, cultivated Gregorian chant, invited learned clergy to teach at Hexham, and corresponded with Bede — who dedicated several of his biblical commentaries to Acca and described him as a lover of learning, Scripture, and music.

Acca was a significant patron of Bede, the greatest scholar of the early Middle Ages, and their friendship and correspondence reveal a flourishing of Christian intellectual life in the kingdom of Northumbria that had no contemporary equal in England. Acca was expelled from Hexham in 732 under circumstances that remain obscure, possibly connected to the political turbulence of Northumbrian royal politics. He is venerated as a saint with a feast day on 20 October.
